title: When Real Speech Is Off-Limits, RL Beats Fine-Tuning on Synthetic Audio
hook: Banks can't just collect real customer speech to adapt voice AI. Trained only on synthetic TTS audio, GRPO cuts word-error rate 40% more than supervised fine-tuning alone.
key_points: In regulated domains like banking, real speech is costly and legally constrained to collect, making synthetic text-to-speech (TTS) audio an attractive but acoustically-mismatched substitute for adapting LLM-based ASR.
Prior work on this synthetic-to-real gap stayed within supervised fine-tuning (SFT); this paper turns to reinforcement learning instead.
GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) — critic-free RL that rewards low-WER hypotheses — extracts far more value from the same synthetic-only speech than SFT.
GRPO alone cuts word-error rate 40% relative to SFT (36.71% to 22.09%); an SFT-then-GRPO combination pushes the reduction to 45%.
The gain traces to behavior change — better stopping calibration and tighter audio-text attention alignment — not to any change in early-layer representations.
content_html: Voice AI in regulated industries like banking faces an awkward catch: real customer speech is exactly the data you'd want to adapt a model on, and exactly the data you're most restricted from collecting. Synthetic text-to-speech is the obvious workaround, but it doesn't sound quite like real audio — and prior work trying to close that gap stuck to ordinary supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
extra_html: Shashi Kumar, Andreas Stolcke, and colleagues instead adapt an LLM-based ASR model with reinforcement learning, using GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) — a critic-free method that rewards hypotheses with lower word-error rate. Trained on the exact same synthetic-only speech, GRPO cuts WER by 40% relative to SFT (36.71% down to 22.09%), and running SFT first followed by GRPO pushes the reduction to 45%. Digging into why, the authors trace the gain to behavior rather than representation: GRPO improves the model's stopping calibration (avoiding insertion errors) and sharpens how its attention aligns audio to text, while early-layer representations stay essentially unchanged. Their takeaway for anyone stuck adapting ASR on synthetic speech alone: reach for reinforcement learning over supervised fine-tuning.

flashcards.prompt: Why is synthetic TTS speech attractive but flawed for adapting ASR in domains like banking?
flashcards.back_html: Real speech is costly and legally constrained to collect there, so synthetic speech is an accessible substitute — but it stays acoustically mismatched with real recordings, limiting how well models trained on it generalize.

flashcards.prompt: What result did GRPO training on synthetic-only speech achieve versus SFT in this paper?

choices.text: 40% relative WER reduction versus SFT alone (36.71% to 22.09%), and 45% with an SFT-then-GRPO combination
GRPO performed identically to SFT since both use the same synthetic data
GRPO only matched SFT when real speech was added to the training set
SFT outperformed GRPO by a wide margin on synthetic-only data

flashcards.explanation_html: Using the same synthetic-only speech, GRPO — a critic-free RL method rewarding low-WER hypotheses — cut WER 40% relative to SFT, and combining SFT with GRPO pushed the reduction to 45%.

flashcards.prompt: Where does GRPO's improvement over SFT actually come from, according to the paper's analysis?
flashcards.back_html: From behavior change, not representation change: GRPO improves stopping calibration and strengthens audio-to-text attention alignment, while leaving early-layer representations largely intact.
